The Weilüe, a Chinese text composed in the early third century CE, describes the Roman Empire (Da Qin) as a vast kingdom located west of Parthia and the Great Sea, accessible by sea from Egypt in as little as two months with favorable winds [S1]. According to this source, the Roman Empire "has more than four hundred smaller cities and towns" and "extends several thousand li in all directions," with its capital city built with stone walls near the mouth of a river [S1]. The Hou Hanshu records that in 166 CE, the king of Da Qin sent envoys bearing elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn, and turtle shell, which the Chinese source notes were "neither precious nor rare," suggesting skepticism about the account [S3]. These Chinese sources present the Roman Empire as a distant, wealthy, and organized state, though one whose tribute offerings seemed unremarkable to Chinese observers.
